Native engine book, chapter 1: the mean structure

Source: vignettes/articles/native-book-1-mean-structure.qmd

This is the first of five chapters that open the native engine and show every matrix it works with. The engine is experimental. The chapters, in order:

  1. The mean structure (this chapter): the RAM form, the implied means, the discrepancy and its gradient, and the moment count.
  2. Scale and conditioning: why the engine fits in centered coordinates and when it may shift the data.
  3. Constrained estimation: constraint rows, the solver, the acceptance gate and the Newton polish.
  4. Fixed exogenous variables: fixed_x, the conditional likelihood and the comparison refusals.
  5. Inference: information, the sandwich, MBCO and anova().

Each chapter fits real models to the bundled mediation_demo data, prints the matrices the engine builds, derives the formulas that produce them, and checks the numbers against lavaan and OpenMx. Each chapter runs on its own.

You need medfit 0.9.0 or later; matrix algebra and the normal likelihood at the level of a first course in multivariate statistics
You get the RAM matrices of a fitted model, the implied mean and covariance computed by hand, the discrepancy and its gradient derived and checked, and the moment and degrees-of-freedom count
Time about 40 minutes 
library(medfit)

Attaching package: 'medfit'
The following object is masked from 'package:stats':

    decompose
f3 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3)
f4 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 4)
mx <- function(x, d = 4) round(x, d)

1. The model

We use the smallest mediation model: a treatment, one mediator and an outcome. Two lines of syntax write the paths, and two more write the intercepts. An intercept statement (y ~ 1) turns on the mean structure: the model then describes the means of the observed variables as well as their covariances. Every observed intercept the text does not write is added and left free, so one intercept line would be enough; the second only makes the model explicit.

syntax <- "
  mediator1 ~ a * treatment
  outcome ~ b * mediator1 + cp * treatment
  mediator1 ~ 1
  outcome ~ 1
"
fit <- fit_sem(syntax, mediation_demo)
ram <- fit@internals$ram
theta <- fit@theta
n <- fit@n_obs
round(theta, 4)
                   a                    b                   cp
              0.4560               0.7134               0.0406
mediator1~~mediator1     outcome~~outcome treatment~~treatment
              1.1585               1.1804               0.2500
         mediator1~1            outcome~1          treatment~1
              0.1552               0.2311               0.5025

theta is the parameter vector: the free parameters in the order the engine keeps them. There are 9 of them: three paths, three variances and three intercepts. treatment is exogenous: no path in the model points to it, so its own mean and variance are parameters, and its “intercept” is its mean. The engine also keeps the model as a RAM specification (fit@internals$ram), which the next section opens.

2. The RAM form: A, S, F and m

RAM stands for reticular action model. It writes every structural equation model with four matrices. Put all the variables of the model, observed and latent, in one vector \(v\) of length \(n_v\). Then the model says

\[ v = A\,v + m + e, \qquad \operatorname{E}(e) = 0, \quad \operatorname{Cov}(e) = S_{\text{ram}} . \]

The pieces are:

  • \(A\), the path matrix (\(n_v \times n_v\)). Entry \(A_{r c}\) is the effect of variable \(c\) on variable \(r\): a one-headed arrow from \(c\) to \(r\).
  • \(m\), the intercept vector (length \(n_v\)). Entry \(m_r\) is the intercept of variable \(r\)’s equation. An exogenous variable’s equation is just its mean, so its intercept is its mean.
  • \(S_{\text{ram}}\), the covariance matrix of the errors (\(n_v \times n_v\)). Its diagonal holds the residual variances (or, for an exogenous variable, its variance); an off-diagonal entry is a two-headed arrow.
  • \(F\), the selection matrix (\(p \times n_v\), with \(p\) the number of observed variables). Each row has one 1 and picks one observed variable out of \(v\).

We read the real matrices of our fit. The helper .sem_ram_mats() builds \(A\) and \(S_{\text{ram}}\) from the parameter vector (it puts each free parameter where the specification says), and .sem_ram_m() builds \(m\):

mats <- medfit:::.sem_ram_mats(ram, theta)
A <- mats$a
Sram <- mats$s
m <- medfit:::.sem_ram_m(ram, theta)
Fsel <- diag(ram$nv)[ram$obs_idx, , drop = FALSE]
dimnames(A) <- dimnames(Sram) <- list(ram$vars, ram$vars)
names(m) <- ram$vars
dimnames(Fsel) <- list(ram$obs, ram$vars)
cat("A (row = target, column = source)\n")
A (row = target, column = source)
mx(A)
          mediator1 treatment outcome
mediator1    0.0000    0.4560       0
treatment    0.0000    0.0000       0
outcome      0.7134    0.0406       0
cat("\nS_ram\n")

S_ram
mx(Sram)
          mediator1 treatment outcome
mediator1    1.1585      0.00  0.0000
treatment    0.0000      0.25  0.0000
outcome      0.0000      0.00  1.1804
cat("\nm\n")

m
mx(m)
mediator1 treatment   outcome
   0.1552    0.5025    0.2311 
cat("\nF\n")

F
Fsel
          mediator1 treatment outcome
mediator1         1         0       0
treatment         0         1       0
outcome           0         0       1

Read \(A\) one row at a time. The row mediator1 has 0.4560 in the treatment column: that is the path \(a\). The row outcome holds \(b\) = 0.7134 and \(c'\) = 0.0406. Every other entry is a structural zero, a path the model does not have. In \(S_{\text{ram}}\) the diagonal is the two residual variances and the variance of treatment; the off-diagonal entries are zero because the model has no correlated errors.

Here every variable is observed, so \(F\) is the identity and does nothing. It earns its place when the model has a latent variable, which sits in \(v\) but not in the data. A mediator measured by two indicators shows it:

latent <- fit_sem("
  M =~ mediator1 + mediator2
  M ~ a * treatment
  outcome ~ b * M + treatment
", mediation_demo, meanstructure = TRUE)
rl <- latent@internals$ram
Fl <- diag(rl$nv)[rl$obs_idx, , drop = FALSE]
dimnames(Fl) <- list(rl$obs, rl$vars)
Fl
          mediator1 mediator2 treatment outcome M
mediator1         1         0         0       0 0
mediator2         0         1         0       0 0
treatment         0         0         1       0 0
outcome           0         0         0       1 0

\(F\) has four rows (the four observed variables) and five columns (those four plus the latent M); the M column is all zeros. From now on we return to the observed model, where \(F = I\).

3. The implied mean and covariance

A fitted model is a claim about the moments of the observed variables: their means \(\mu\) and covariance matrix \(\Sigma\). We derive both from the RAM equation.

Step 1: solve for \(v\). Move \(A v\) to the left: \((I - A)v = m + e\). The matrix \(I - A\) is invertible when the model has no feedback loop. The engine gives a parameter vector that makes it singular (or that makes the implied covariance not positive definite) a large finite discrepancy, so the optimizer steps back from it. Write \(B = (I - A)^{-1}\), so

\[ v = B\,(m + e). \]

Step 2: take the expectation. \(B\) and \(m\) are constants and \(\operatorname{E}(e) = 0\), so \(\operatorname{E}(v) = B\,m\).

Step 3: take the covariance. \(\operatorname{Cov}(v) = B \operatorname{Cov}(e) B^\top = B\,S_{\text{ram}}\,B^\top\), because \(\operatorname{Cov}(M x) = M \operatorname{Cov}(x) M^\top\) for a constant matrix \(M\) and the constant \(m\) adds nothing to a covariance.

Step 4: select the observed variables. The data contain only the observed rows of \(v\), which is what multiplying by \(F\) does:

\[ \mu(\theta) = F\,(I - A)^{-1} m, \qquad \Sigma(\theta) = F\,(I - A)^{-1} S_{\text{ram}} (I - A)^{-\top} F^\top . \]

Now push the numbers through. First \(B\):

B <- solve(diag(ram$nv) - A)
mx(B)
          mediator1 treatment outcome
mediator1    1.0000    0.4560       0
treatment    0.0000    1.0000       0
outcome      0.7134    0.3659       1

Column treatment of \(B\) reads: a one-unit change in treatment moves mediator1 by \(a\) = 0.4560 and outcome by \(a b + c'\) = 0.3659. That is the total effect, the sum of the indirect path \(a b\) = 0.3253 and the direct path. \(B\) collects every path from one variable to another.

mu <- drop(Fsel %*% B %*% m)
Sigma <- Fsel %*% B %*% Sram %*% t(B) %*% t(Fsel)
cat("mu\n")
mu
mx(mu)
mediator1 treatment   outcome
   0.3843    0.5025    0.5257 
cat("\nSigma\n")

Sigma
mx(Sigma)
          mediator1 treatment outcome
mediator1    1.2105    0.1140  0.8682
treatment    0.1140    0.2500  0.0915
outcome      0.8682    0.0915  1.8036
# the engine's own helpers, and the largest absolute difference from the hand computation
c(
  mean = max(abs(medfit:::.sem_implied_mean(ram, theta) - mu)),
  cov = max(abs(medfit:::.sem_implied(ram, theta) - Sigma))
)
mean  cov
   0    0

The last two numbers are the largest absolute differences between our matrix product and the engine’s helpers, so they would be large if either side had an error. This model has as many free parameters as observed moments (Section 6 counts them) and is identified, so it can match any sample means and covariances. Compare with the sample moments:

x <- as.matrix(fit@data[, ram$obs])
xbar <- colMeans(x)
S <- cov(x) * (n - 1) / n
cat("sample mean\n")
sample mean
mx(xbar)
mediator1 treatment   outcome
   0.3843    0.5025    0.5257 
cat("\nsample covariance (divisor n)\n")

sample covariance (divisor n)
mx(S)
          mediator1 treatment outcome
mediator1    1.2105    0.1140  0.8682
treatment    0.1140    0.2500  0.0915
outcome      0.8682    0.0915  1.8036
c(mean = max(abs(mu - xbar)), cov = max(abs(Sigma - S)))
        mean          cov
1.110223e-16 2.220446e-16

The model reproduces the sample mean and covariance to rounding. An identified model with as many free parameters as observed moments (zero degrees of freedom) is saturated: it reproduces every data set this way, so it cannot be rejected.

4. The discrepancy

The engine finds \(\theta\) by maximum likelihood. This section derives the function it minimizes, including the term the mean structure adds.

Setup. The data are \(n\) rows \(x_1, \dots, x_n\), each a vector of the \(p\) observed variables, assumed independent and multivariate normal with mean \(\mu\) and covariance \(\Sigma\). The density of one row is

\[ f(x_i) = (2\pi)^{-p/2} |\Sigma|^{-1/2} \exp\left\{ -\tfrac12 (x_i - \mu)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (x_i - \mu) \right\}. \]

Step 1: the log likelihood. Rows are independent, so the log likelihood is the sum of the log densities:

\[ -2 \log L = n p \log 2\pi + n \log|\Sigma| + \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \mu)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (x_i - \mu). \]

Step 2: split each deviation. Write \(x_i - \mu = (x_i - \bar x) + d\), with \(\bar x\) the sample mean and \(d = \bar x - \mu\) the gap between the sample mean and the model’s mean. Expanding the quadratic form gives three terms:

\[ \sum_i (x_i - \bar x)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (x_i - \bar x) + 2\, d^\top \Sigma^{-1} \sum_i (x_i - \bar x) + n\, d^\top \Sigma^{-1} d . \]

The middle term is zero, because deviations from the sample mean sum to zero (\(\sum_i (x_i - \bar x) = 0\)).

Step 3: turn the first sum into a trace. A scalar equals its own trace, and \(\operatorname{tr}(u^\top M u) = \operatorname{tr}(M u u^\top)\), so \(\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (x_i - \bar x) = \operatorname{tr}\bigl(\Sigma^{-1} \sum_i (x_i - \bar x)(x_i - \bar x)^\top\bigr) = n \operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{-1} S)\), with \(S\) the sample covariance with divisor \(n\) (the engine’s choice, which is the maximum likelihood estimate).

Step 4: collect.

\[ -2 \log L = n \left[ p \log 2\pi + \log|\Sigma| + \operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{-1} S) + d^\top \Sigma^{-1} d \right]. \]

Step 5: scale to a discrepancy. The engine minimizes the function that is this bracket with the saturated value subtracted. The saturated model sets \(\mu = \bar x\) and \(\Sigma = S\), giving \(d = 0\) and a bracket of \(p \log 2\pi + \log|S| + \operatorname{tr}(I) = p\log 2\pi + \log|S| + p\). Subtracting it leaves

\[ F_{ML}(\theta) = \log|\Sigma| + \operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{-1} S) - \log|S| - p + \underbrace{(\bar x - \mu)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (\bar x - \mu)}_{\text{mean term}}, \qquad -2\log L = n \left( F_{ML} + \log|S| + p + p \log 2\pi \right). \]

Two facts follow. First, \(F_{ML} \ge 0\), with equality exactly when the model reproduces the sample mean and covariance (a saturated model always does). The proof is short. The mean term is a quadratic form in a positive definite matrix, so it is nonnegative. For the rest, let \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_p\) be the eigenvalues of \(\Sigma^{-1} S\), all positive because \(S\) is positive definite (the engine requires it). \(\Sigma^{-1} S\) is similar to the symmetric matrix \(\Sigma^{-1/2} S \Sigma^{-1/2}\), so all \(\lambda_j = 1\) means \(\Sigma = S\). Then \(\log|\Sigma| - \log|S| = -\sum_j \log\lambda_j\) and \(\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{-1} S) = \sum_j \lambda_j\), so the covariance part equals \(\sum_j (\lambda_j - \log \lambda_j - 1)\). Each term is nonnegative, because \(\log \lambda \le \lambda - 1\), and it is zero only at \(\lambda = 1\). Second, \(n F_{ML}\) is the likelihood-ratio statistic against the saturated model, since the saturated model’s \(-2\log L\) is the bracket with \(F_{ML} = 0\); that is why it is the model chi-square. Without a mean structure the means are free, \(d = 0\), and the mean term is absent: that is the whole of the extension.

Worked instance. Our free model is saturated, so \(F_{ML} = 0\) and there is nothing to see. Fix the outcome’s intercept at zero with outcome ~ 0*1 and the model can no longer match the outcome mean. Section 6 returns to what the restriction means; for now it gives a nonzero \(F_{ML}\) to take apart.

syntax0 <- sub("outcome ~ 1", "outcome ~ 0*1", syntax, fixed = TRUE)
fit0 <- fit_sem(syntax0, mediation_demo)
ram0 <- fit0@internals$ram
th0 <- fit0@theta
Sigma0 <- medfit:::.sem_implied(ram0, th0)
mu0 <- medfit:::.sem_implied_mean(ram0, th0)
d <- xbar - mu0
Sinv <- solve(Sigma0)
p <- length(xbar)

cov_part <- log(det(Sigma0)) + sum(diag(Sinv %*% S)) - log(det(S)) - p
mean_part <- drop(t(d) %*% Sinv %*% d)
c(covariance = cov_part, mean = mean_part, total = cov_part + mean_part, engine = fit0@f)
covariance       mean      total     engine
0.01130355 0.01073159 0.02203514 0.02203514

The gap vector \(d = \bar x - \mu\) shows where the restriction bites:

mx(d)
mediator1 treatment   outcome
   0.0000    0.0000    0.1138

The model matches the sample means of mediator1 and treatment (their intercepts are free) and misses the outcome mean by 0.114. Both parts of the discrepancy are positive, which is worth a moment. The paths \(b\) and \(c'\) appear in the covariance and in the outcome mean at once, so the optimizer moves them away from the values that match the covariance exactly (compare \(b\) = 0.7287 here with 0.7134 in the free fit) to close part of the mean gap, and pays for it in the covariance part. The two terms trade off; their sum is what is minimized.

The log likelihood follows from the same pieces. Summing the log density row by row, with no shortcut, must agree with logLik(), which uses the formula in step 5:

ll_rows <- sum(vapply(seq_len(n), function(i) {
  di <- x[i, ] - mu0
  -0.5 * (p * log(2 * pi) + log(det(Sigma0)) + drop(t(di) %*% Sinv %*% di))
}, numeric(1)))
ll_formula <- -0.5 * n * (fit0@f + log(det(S)) + p + p * log(2 * pi))
c(row_by_row = ll_rows, formula = ll_formula, logLik = as.numeric(logLik(fit0)))
row_by_row    formula     logLik
 -1492.468  -1492.468  -1492.468

5. The gradient

The optimizer needs \(\partial F_{ML} / \partial \theta_k\). The engine supplies it analytically. This section derives it in four steps, and then checks each factor against finite differences.

Step 1: the matrix calculus. For a symmetric positive definite \(\Sigma\), \(\partial \log|\Sigma| = \operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{-1} \partial\Sigma)\) and \(\partial \Sigma^{-1} = -\Sigma^{-1} (\partial\Sigma) \Sigma^{-1}\). The first is Jacobi’s formula; the second follows from differentiating \(\Sigma\Sigma^{-1} = I\). By the cyclic property of the trace, \(d^\top \Sigma^{-1} d = \operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{-1} d d^\top)\), so the mean term can be treated as a trace too. Write \(S_{\text{eff}} = S + d d^\top\), so that holding \(d\) fixed,

\[ \partial F_{ML} = \operatorname{tr}\bigl(\Sigma^{-1} \partial\Sigma\bigr) - \operatorname{tr}\bigl(\Sigma^{-1} S_{\text{eff}} \Sigma^{-1} \partial\Sigma\bigr) + (\text{change through } d). \]

Step 2: the change through \(d\). \(d = \bar x - \mu\), so \(\partial d = -\partial\mu\) (the sample mean does not depend on \(\theta\)) and \(\partial (d^\top \Sigma^{-1} d)|_{\Sigma\ \text{fixed}} = -2\, (\partial\mu)^\top \Sigma^{-1} d\). Together:

\[ \frac{\partial F_{ML}}{\partial \theta_k} = \operatorname{tr}\bigl(W\, \partial_k \Sigma\bigr) - 2\, (\partial_k \mu)^\top \Sigma^{-1} d, \qquad W = \Sigma^{-1} - \Sigma^{-1} S_{\text{eff}} \Sigma^{-1}. \]

Step 3: the derivative of \(B\). To get \(\partial_k\Sigma\) and \(\partial_k\mu\) we need how \(B = (I - A)^{-1}\) moves. Differentiate \(B (I - A) = I\): \((\partial B)(I - A) - B\,\partial A = 0\), so \(\partial B = B\,(\partial A)\,B\).

Step 4: the derivative of the moments. Let \(e_r\) be the \(r\)th unit vector.

  • A path entry \(A_{r c}\) has \(\partial A = e_r e_c^\top\), hence \(\partial B = B e_r e_c^\top B\). Then \(\partial \mu = F B e_r \,(B m)_c\) and \(\partial \Sigma_{\text{full}} = B e_r e_c^\top B\, S_{\text{ram}} B^\top + \text{its transpose}\), where \(\Sigma_{\text{full}} = B S_{\text{ram}} B^\top\) is the covariance of all of \(v\).
  • An intercept \(m_j\) moves \(\mu\) by \(F B e_j\) and does not touch \(\Sigma\).
  • A variance or covariance entry \((S_{\text{ram}})_{r c}\) has \(\partial \Sigma_{\text{full}} = B e_r e_c^\top B^\top\) (plus its transpose when \(r \neq c\), because the matrix is symmetric and the two entries are one parameter) and does not touch \(\mu\).

Two parameters with the same label are one parameter, so their contributions add. The engine’s .sem_dsigma() and .sem_dmu() return these derivatives; we check them against central differences of .sem_implied() and .sem_implied_mean(), which know nothing about the algebra above:

central <- function(f, theta, k, h = 1e-6) {
  up <- dn <- theta
  up[k] <- theta[k] + h
  dn[k] <- theta[k] - h
  (f(up) - f(dn)) / (2 * h)
}
dsig <- medfit:::.sem_dsigma(th0, ram0)
dmu <- medfit:::.sem_dmu(th0, ram0)
err_sigma <- vapply(seq_along(th0), function(k) {
  max(abs(dsig[[k]] - central(function(t) medfit:::.sem_implied(ram0, t), th0, k)))
}, numeric(1))
err_mu <- vapply(seq_along(th0), function(k) {
  max(abs(dmu[, k] - central(function(t) medfit:::.sem_implied_mean(ram0, t), th0, k)))
}, numeric(1))
signif(cbind(sigma = err_sigma, mu = err_mu), 2) |> `rownames<-`(names(th0))
                       sigma      mu
a                    7.8e-11 4.6e-11
b                    5.7e-11 3.1e-11
cp                   6.4e-11 2.9e-11
mediator1~~mediator1 8.2e-11 0.0e+00
outcome~~outcome     8.2e-11 0.0e+00
treatment~~treatment 9.3e-11 0.0e+00
mediator1~1          0.0e+00 6.9e-12
treatment~1          0.0e+00 3.6e-11

Each row is a free parameter and each entry is the largest absolute discrepancy between the analytic derivative and the finite difference, so a wrong derivative would show as a number near the size of the derivative itself. Now the whole gradient. At the optimum it must vanish. At another point it must match a finite difference of \(F_{ML}\) itself, so we test it at the engine’s starting value, where the gradient is large:

smp <- medfit:::.sem_sample(fit0@data, ram0)
grad_formula <- function(theta) {
  Sg <- medfit:::.sem_implied(ram0, theta)
  mug <- medfit:::.sem_implied_mean(ram0, theta)
  Si <- solve(Sg)
  dg <- smp$xbar - mug
  W <- Si - Si %*% (smp$s + tcrossprod(dg)) %*% Si
  ds <- medfit:::.sem_dsigma(theta, ram0)
  dm <- medfit:::.sem_dmu(theta, ram0)
  vapply(seq_along(theta), function(k) {
    sum(W * ds[[k]]) - 2 * drop(crossprod(dm[, k], Si %*% dg))
  }, numeric(1))
}
start <- medfit:::.sem_default_start(ram0, smp)
fml <- function(t) medfit:::.sem_fml(t, ram0, smp)
fd <- vapply(seq_along(start), function(k) central(fml, start, k), numeric(1))
signif(cbind(
  formula = grad_formula(start),
  finite_difference = fd,
  engine = medfit:::.sem_grad(start, ram0, smp)
), 4) |> `rownames<-`(names(start))
                        formula finite_difference     engine
a                    -1.949e-01           -0.1949 -1.949e-01
b                    -1.823e+00           -1.8230 -1.823e+00
cp                   -4.062e-01           -0.4062 -4.062e-01
mediator1~~mediator1 -1.548e+00           -1.5480 -1.548e+00
outcome~~outcome     -9.868e-01           -0.9868 -9.868e-01
treatment~~treatment -8.000e+00           -8.0000 -8.000e+00
mediator1~1          -6.798e-18            0.0000 -3.455e-17
treatment~1          -1.027e-17            0.0000  4.524e-17
c(at_start_vs_fd = max(abs(grad_formula(start) - fd)),
  at_optimum = max(abs(grad_formula(th0))))
at_start_vs_fd     at_optimum
  1.019632e-09   4.024558e-16

The three columns agree. The last two rows, the intercepts of mediator1 and treatment, are zero for a reason worth seeing. The default start sets these two intercepts so that the implied means of mediator1 and treatment equal their sample means, which leaves a gap only in the outcome: \(d = d_y e_y\). With every variable observed, \(\Sigma^{-1} = (I - A)^\top S_{\text{ram}}^{-1} (I - A)\). The outcome causes nothing, so \((I - A) e_y = e_y\), and its residual is uncorrelated with the others, so \(S_{\text{ram}}^{-1} e_y = e_y / s_y\) with \(s_y\) its residual variance. Hence \(\Sigma^{-1} d = (d_y / s_y)(I - A)^\top e_y\), and the gradient of intercept \(m_j\), which is \(-2\,(B e_j)^\top \Sigma^{-1} d\) by Step 2 and Step 4, equals \(-2\,(d_y / s_y)\, e_j^\top B^\top (I - A)^\top e_y = -2\,(d_y/s_y)\, e_j^\top e_y = 0\) for every \(j\) other than the outcome. At the optimum every component of the gradient is numerically zero: the fit sits at a stationary point.

6. Counting moments and degrees of freedom

The data summarize to \(p\) means and \(p(p+1)/2\) distinct variances and covariances, so a model with a mean structure faces \(p(p+3)/2\) observed moments. Here \(p = 3\) gives 9 moments. The degrees of freedom are the moments minus the free parameters,

\[ \text{df} = \frac{p(p+1)}{2} + p - q , \]

with \(q\) the number of free parameters after equality constraints (Chapter 3). The free model has \(q\) = 9, so df = 0: saturated, as Section 3 found. Fixing the outcome intercept removes one parameter and no moment:

data.frame(
  model = c("all intercepts free", "outcome ~ 0*1"),
  moments = c(medfit:::.sem_moments(ram), medfit:::.sem_moments(ram0)),
  free_parameters = c(ram$q, ram0$q),
  df = c(fit@df, fit0@df),
  chisq = round(c(n * fit@f, n * fit0@f), 4)
)
                model moments free_parameters df  chisq
1 all intercepts free       9               9  0 0.0000
2       outcome ~ 0*1       9               8  1 8.8141

So y ~ 0*1 is a one-degree-of-freedom restriction, and its chi-square is \(n F_{ML}\) = 8.814, the number Section 4 took apart. What does it test? With the outcome intercept at zero, the outcome mean is no longer free: the RAM equation forces \(\mu_y = b\,\mu_{m} + c'\,\mu_x\), the mean carried by the mediator and the treatment through the paths. The data can contradict that, and the restriction asks whether they do. anova(), the subject of Chapter 5, turns the same quantity into a p-value:

anova(fit0, fit)
Likelihood-ratio (chi-square difference) test for SEMFit models

n = 400; Chisq is n times the minimized discrepancy

     Df  Chisq Chisq diff Df diff Pr(>Chisq)
fit   0 0.0000
fit0  1 8.8141     8.8141       1   0.002989 **
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

A Wald test of the same hypothesis reads the free fit’s intercept and its standard error, \(z = \hat m_y / \operatorname{SE}(\hat m_y)\):

est <- theta["outcome~1"]
se <- sqrt(diag(fit@vcov))["outcome~1"]
c(intercept = unname(est), se = unname(se), wald_chisq = unname((est / se)^2),
  lr_chisq = n * fit0@f)
 intercept         se wald_chisq   lr_chisq
0.23110834 0.07741603 8.91188286 8.81405616

The Wald and likelihood-ratio statistics are two standard ways to test one parameter. They agree in large samples and differ in finite ones: here 8.912 against 8.814.

7. Cross-checks: lavaan and OpenMx

Both packages fit the restricted model to the same data. lavaan reports the chi-square, the degrees of freedom and the log likelihood directly. We set meanstructure = TRUE and fixed.x = FALSE so that it estimates the exogenous mean and variance the way the native engine does (Chapter 4 explains the alternative).

lv <- lavaan::sem("
  mediator1 ~ a * treatment
  outcome ~ b * mediator1 + cp * treatment
  outcome ~ 0 * 1
", data = mediation_demo, meanstructure = TRUE, fixed.x = FALSE)
est_lv <- lavaan::coef(lv)
est_mf <- coef(fit0)
common <- intersect(names(est_lv), names(est_mf))
data.frame(
  quantity = c("chisq", "df", "logLik"),
  medfit = c(n * fit0@f, fit0@df, as.numeric(logLik(fit0))),
  lavaan = c(lavaan::fitMeasures(lv, "chisq"), lavaan::fitMeasures(lv, "df"),
             lavaan::fitMeasures(lv, "logl"))
)
      quantity       medfit       lavaan
chisq    chisq     8.814056     8.814056
df          df     1.000000     1.000000
logl    logLik -1492.467976 -1492.467976
c(coefficients_compared = length(common),
  largest_absolute_difference = max(abs(est_lv[common] - est_mf[common])))
      coefficients_compared largest_absolute_difference
               8.000000e+00                5.694416e-10

The second result is the largest absolute difference over the coefficients the two fits share.

OpenMx fits the same model on the raw data. Its RAM interface mirrors the matrices of Section 2: mxPath with arrows = 1 fills \(A\), arrows = 2 fills \(S_{\text{ram}}\), and a path from "one" fills \(m\). The outcome’s intercept path is fixed at 0.

suppressMessages(library(OpenMx))
mxOption(NULL, "Number of Threads", 1)
dat <- mediation_demo[, c("mediator1", "treatment", "outcome")]
vars <- names(dat)
mod <- mxModel(
  "restricted", type = "RAM", manifestVars = vars,
  mxPath(from = "treatment", to = "mediator1", values = 0.4, labels = "a"),
  mxPath(from = c("mediator1", "treatment"), to = "outcome", values = 0.5, labels = c("b", "cp")),
  mxPath(from = vars, arrows = 2, values = 1, labels = paste0("v_", vars)),
  mxPath(from = "one", to = c("mediator1", "treatment"), values = 0, labels = c("m_m", "m_t")),
  mxPath(from = "one", to = "outcome", free = FALSE, values = 0),
  mxData(dat, type = "raw")
)
run <- mxRun(mod, silent = TRUE)
smry <- summary(run)
est_mx <- stats::setNames(smry$parameters$Estimate, smry$parameters$name)
mx_map <- c(a = "a", b = "b", cp = "cp", "mediator1~~mediator1" = "v_mediator1",
            "outcome~~outcome" = "v_outcome", "treatment~~treatment" = "v_treatment",
            "mediator1~1" = "m_m", "treatment~1" = "m_t")
data.frame(quantity = "-2 log L", medfit = -2 * as.numeric(logLik(fit0)),
           OpenMx = smry$Minus2LogLikelihood)
  quantity   medfit   OpenMx
1 -2 log L 2984.936 2984.936
c(largest_absolute_difference = max(abs(est_mx[mx_map] - est_mf[names(mx_map)])))
largest_absolute_difference
               1.050627e-06 
c(OpenMx_degreesOfFreedom = smry$degreesOfFreedom, data_values_n_times_p = n * p,
  free_parameters = nrow(smry$parameters), saturated_moments = medfit:::.sem_moments(ram0),
  medfit_df = fit0@df)
OpenMx_degreesOfFreedom   data_values_n_times_p         free_parameters
                   1192                    1200                       8
      saturated_moments               medfit_df
                      9                       1

The two -2 log L values agree; the coefficients agree less closely than lavaan’s, a difference in where the two optimizers stop.

The last line shows that OpenMx’s degreesOfFreedom is a different count. For raw data OpenMx subtracts the number of free parameters from the number of observed data values, \(n p\). The chi-square degrees of freedom compare against the saturated model, which has \(p(p+3)/2\) parameters, so they are the saturated moments minus the free parameters, the engine’s fit0@df.

8. The information is a sum

One more consequence of the mean structure, used in Chapter 5. The score of one row is the gradient of its log density with respect to \(\theta\). The expected information of \(n\) independent rows is \(n\) times the covariance matrix of one row’s score (its definition; for a likelihood regular enough to differentiate under the integral it also equals the expected negative Hessian, Chapter 5). Under normality it is the sum of a covariance part and a mean part with no cross term:

\[ I_{kl} = \frac{n}{2} \operatorname{tr}\bigl(\Sigma^{-1} \partial_k\Sigma\, \Sigma^{-1} \partial_l\Sigma\bigr) + n\, (\partial_k \mu)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (\partial_l \mu). \]

Why. Write \(u = x_i - \mu\), so \(u \sim N(0, \Sigma)\). Differentiating the log density \(-\tfrac12\bigl[\log|\Sigma| + u^\top \Sigma^{-1} u\bigr]\) (the same calculus as Section 5, with \(\partial u = -\partial\mu\)) gives the score of one row in two parts,

\[ s_k = \underbrace{(\partial_k\mu)^\top \Sigma^{-1} u}_{\text{mean part, linear in } u} + \underbrace{\tfrac12\bigl[u^\top \Sigma^{-1} (\partial_k\Sigma)\, \Sigma^{-1} u - \operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{-1}\partial_k\Sigma)\bigr]}_{\text{covariance part, quadratic in } u}. \]

Cross term: the covariance of a linear and a quadratic function of \(u\) involves third-order moments of \(u\), which are zero because the normal distribution is symmetric about its mean. Mean part: \(\operatorname{Cov}\bigl((\partial_k\mu)^\top \Sigma^{-1} u,\, (\partial_l\mu)^\top \Sigma^{-1} u\bigr) = (\partial_k\mu)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (\partial_l\mu)\), since \(\operatorname{Cov}(u) = \Sigma\). Covariance part: for symmetric \(M, N\), the normal moment identity \(\operatorname{Cov}(u^\top M u,\, u^\top N u) = 2\operatorname{tr}(M\Sigma N\Sigma)\) with \(M = \tfrac12\Sigma^{-1}\partial_k\Sigma\,\Sigma^{-1}\) and \(N = \tfrac12\Sigma^{-1}\partial_l\Sigma\,\Sigma^{-1}\) gives \(\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{-1}\partial_k\Sigma\,\Sigma^{-1}\partial_l\Sigma)\). Multiplying by \(n\) gives the two terms above. Check the result against the engine, which computes the same two terms:

sigma_inv <- solve(Sigma0)
cov_info <- 0.5 * n * outer(seq_along(th0), seq_along(th0), Vectorize(function(k, l) {
  sum(diag(sigma_inv %*% dsig[[k]] %*% sigma_inv %*% dsig[[l]]))
}))
mean_info <- n * crossprod(dmu, sigma_inv %*% dmu)
info_hand <- cov_info + mean_info
info_engine <- medfit:::.sem_info_expected(th0, ram0, smp, NULL)
c(difference = max(abs(info_hand - info_engine)), largest_entry = max(abs(info_engine)))
   difference largest_entry
 4.547474e-13  3.200160e+03

The hand-built information matches the engine’s. Its inverse estimates the covariance matrix of the estimates; the engine’s default uses the observed information instead (Chapter 5 compares the two), and Chapter 2 shows why the inverse needs a change of coordinates when the means are large.

Check yourself

  1. In the RAM form, which matrix would you change to add a correlation between two residuals? Which to add a path from the treatment to a new mediator? (Answer: \(S_{\text{ram}}\), then \(A\).)
  2. A model with \(p = 4\) observed variables, a mean structure and 12 free parameters has how many degrees of freedom? (Answer: \(4 \cdot 5 / 2 + 4 - 12 = 2\).)
  3. Why is the middle term in Step 2 of Section 4 zero, and what would break if \(\bar x\) were replaced by some other center? (Answer: deviations from the sample mean sum to zero; for another center the cross term would not vanish and the likelihood would not split into a covariance part and a mean part.)

Where next

Chapter 2 asks what happens to this machinery when the variables sit far from zero relative to their spread, and shows why the engine fits in centered coordinates.
